Data Intensive Systems 2026-2027 course project

Data Reduction in Graph Databases

The goal of this project is to develop and evaluate a data reduction method that identifies the most valuable graphs in a graph database for a given query log. The idea is that such a tool can be used to enhance the functionality of a graph database. The implementation has to be in Apache Spark and investigate how well the reduced database preserves query answers.
# Data Reduction
We collect so much data that we often run out of storage space and need to delete some of it. How should we decide which data to delete? This is the challenge of data reduction. Recent works have investigated data reduction for tabular data. The following papers provide background: [Background paper in the EDBT 2023 proceedings](https://openproceedings.org/2023/conf/edbt/3-paper-64.pdf), [Background paper on data reduction from SIGMOD2026](https://velgias.github.io/docs/RicoSV26.pdf)

Instead, in this project, the goal is to investigate and develop a solution for graph data. Given a graph database and a set of queries on it, your method should identify the portions of the database that are most important.
# A Graph Data Model
A graph consists of a set of nodes and a set of edges.

Each node has a unique identifier, which is used to reference it. For simplicity, assume that node identifiers are numeric.

An edge connects   string. It is modelled as a triple ⟨s, l, d⟩, where s and d are the identifiers of the source and destination nodes, respectively, and l is the edge label. For example, <5, "married", 7> represents an edge from node 5 to node 7 with the label "married". For readability, we will omit quotation marks around edge labels and write <5, married, 7>. Labels are single words consisting only of letters and numbers, with no spaces or punctuation.

Nodes may have attributes. An attribute is a name–value pair, such as "city":"Utrecht". We will omit quotation marks around attribute names, so this will be written as city:"Utrecht".

An attribute value is always a string, even when it represents a number, and must therefore always be enclosed in quotation marks. For example, we will write age:"5" and not age:5.

A graph can be represented as a set of triples, i.e., three elements. Each triple starts with < and ends with >. A triple identifies either an edge or an attribute of a node. The first element is always a number and identifies a node. If the third element is a number, the triple represents an edge from the node identified by the first element to the node identified by the third. In that case the second element is the edge label. If the third element is a string, the triple represents an attribute of the node identified by the first element. The second element is the attribute name, and the third is its value. For example the attribute city:"Utrecht" of the node 3 is modelled as <3,city,”Utrecht”>.

A raw representing a graph contains all the triples one after the other separated by a comma. For instance, the graph below:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Is modelled as: 

`<``1,top``,2``>``,``<2,right``,3``>``,``<3,bottom``,4``>``,``<4,left``,1``>``,``<1,isBoss``,"yes">`

A graph path is a sequence of the form *x*1.*x*2.*x*3…*x*n, where each *x*i is called a component of the path. Components can be node identifiers or edge labels, subject to the following rules:

• The first component, *x*1, must always be a node identifier.

• The last component, *x*n, can be a node identifier, an edge label, or a string.

• If *x*n is a string, *x*n−1 must be an attribute name and *x*n−2 must be a node identifier.

• If *x*i is a node identifier and there is a following component, *x*i+1 must be an edge label.

A graph satisfies a path *x*1.*x*2.*x*3…*x*n if, starting at node *x*1, it is possible to traverse the graph following nodes and edges, possibly ending with an attribute name and value, according to the path sequence.

For example, consider the following path: `5.married``.``7.city``."Amsterdam"`

A graph satisfies this path if node 5 has an edge labelled married to node 7, and node 7 has an attribute named city with the value "Amsterdam". The node ids may be also variables. For instance, you can have the following path: : `5.married``.``X``.city``.``Y``  which means starting from node 5 goes to some node  ``(the X)``  through a married edge, and from that node, through  ``a``  city edge to another node ``  (the Y). `` `

 A query is a set of graph paths. A graph satisfies a query if it satisfies every path in that query. If it satisfies some, but not all, of the paths, it partially satisfies the query.

A query log is a text file containing a set of queries, one query per line. Each query is expressed by listing its paths on the same line, separated by commas.

A graph database, or simply a database, is a collection of graphs.
# Problem Statement
Imagine that you are working for Neo4j, a well-known graph database company, and have been asked to develop a data reduction module, because neo4J does not support yet such a functionality.

Given a graph database D and a query log Q, and a number BÎ[0,1], your module must select a reduced database D’ÍD, such that |D′| =B*|D| and best serves Q. A query log Q is best served if the answers to its query are least affected by the consideration of the subset D’ instead of the whole D. |D| and |D’| denotes the number of graphs in the database D and D’, respectively. The database and query log are supplied in two files, Database.txt and QLog.txt. 
## Required work
1. Develop a method for measuring the value or importance of a graph g ∈ D, given the database D and query log Q.

2. Develop a program in Apache Spark that computes the importance of the graphs in D and selects the B% most valuable graphs, where B is the third input parameter.

3. Design, execute, measure, and present experiments that demonstrate how well your module works. Decide which tests to run, how many to run, and which datasets to use. As an employee developing a module in Neo4J for future customers, you do not know who those customers will be or how they will use it. You must therefore develop suitable datasets and query logs. In addition, test your system on two datasets that will be provided to you.

4. Create a dataset and a query log that you believe are rich enough to demonstrate how well a system performs and share them with the class as specified in the deliverables.

5. Write a theory section describing your method from item 1 in detail and explaining the reasons for your choices.

6. Write an implementation section describing how you implemented the method in Apache Spark.

7. Write an experimentation section describing the experiments you conducted and your findings.

8. Within the experimentation section, describe your system’s performance on the two provided datasets. Comment on the quality of these datasets, explain your assessment, and describe your experience using them.
